title: Large-scale refactoring with parity proof
subtitle: Rewrite a system, prove it is the same system. My governance platform's own refactors carry parity proofs, and the largest example is a GPU runtime ported to C++ without changing a token.

stats.label: domain modules the two oversized files became
tests moved alongside the code they cover
shell hooks ported to one Rust binary
exact cells bit for bit at the C++ port, 12 of 12 compressed

lede: AgentOS: the AgentOS store and admin CLI had grown into two very large Rust files, and I had them split into domain modules. The parity proof came from a separate witness seat. Test counts are taken before a refactor, so "all green" is measured against the original code, and comparing exported symbols in the witness's own release builds catches an accidental API removal while confirming the intended demotions to private. A failed proof is not amended; it is replaced by a new proof that names the problems it resolved. The hook layer, through which AgentOS turns policy into refusals inside coding-agent sessions, went through the same discipline.
quote: I decided the split was finished only when someone who had not done it could show it was the same system.
evidence: C++ and native ports with parity proof: a GPU serving runtime ported from Python to native C++ without changing a token, 13 of 13 exact cells and 12 of 12 compressed cells bit for bit.
Large-scale refactoring: two Rust files of about 40,300 and 42,500 lines split into 21 domain modules, with 430+ tests moved alongside the code they cover.
Parity proof by an independent witness: a seat that did not do the work took test baselines, built its own release binaries and compared exported symbols before and after.
Rust systems engineering: 63 shell hooks ported to one Rust binary, tested against fake hook contexts and published byte for byte.
author: Corey James
